metadata.title: I built Canada’s largest crypto company. But the business climate here made selling to Robinhood inevitable

content.text:
I built Canada’s largest crypto company. But the business climate here made selling to Robinhood inevitable
When Robinhood agreed to buy WonderFi, the company I founded, some of Canada's loudest voices argued that federal regulators should block the deal. WonderFi, they said, had become a strategic national asset, the crypto equivalent of one of Canada's Big Five banks, and that it could not be allowed to fall into American hands.
I understood the concern. Canada has been losing on too many fronts. For decades, capital and many of our most talented and ambitious citizens have moved south. But blocking the sale of my company to Robinhood would have done nothing to address the underlying problems that have spurred this exodus.
Sure, Canada would be better off with more large, Canadian-owned tech companies. But that would require creating the conditions for a company as ambitious as WonderFi to keep expanding after winning the home market.
I founded WonderFi in 2021. Over the next several years, we brought together the best talent and technology in the country, built a national brand, and consolidated a fragmented crypto market. We built trust with millions of users – no small feat after Quadriga, Canada's last notable crypto exchange, collapsed in fraud and scandal. We went on to survive the collapse of FTX, despite them being an early investor, and worked through one of the most aggressive regulatory overhauls any crypto market had seen. By 2023, we owned the Canadian market.
I'm proud of what we built, but winning Canada was never supposed to be the end. I wanted WonderFi to become an international success. But the most credible path to global scale came through Robinhood, which saw WonderFi as its entry point into the Canadian market and acquired the company for C$250 million—an excellent outcome for WonderFi and a clear step into its next phase of growth.
Canada's growth ceiling
Canada claims to have an innovation culture. The reality is much different. Canada has created a ceiling for growth for ambitious companies. This didn't happen all at once but gradually as entrepreneurs confronted an interlocking series of headwinds: weaker business investment, thinner growth capital, declining public markets, fragmented regulation and less competitive reward for taking risk.
Other countries are moving aggressively in the opposite direction. Florida and Texas compete tooth and nail for founders and investors (no state income tax). At the federal level, the United States gives founders and early investors major capital gains exclusions. Britain and Singapore offer strong incentives for local investors and innovation. In contrast, Canada offers a patchwork of programs, credits and consultations, which are layered onto higher taxes, scarce capital and sluggish policy-making. In a relatively small market, that makes the risk-reward equation worse. Canada has not competed with the same urgency.
